title: Fathers are fallible witnesses — their consensus cannot equal inspired Scripture
source_text: XXXVI. Et certe quam immerito traditiones non scriptae authoritate cum Scriptura aequantur, inde manifestum est, quod in Scripturis sacris Christum Dominum hoc & illud docuisse, atque instituisse testantur nobis Scriptores divinitus inspirati, & extra omne erroris periculum positi. Sed de dictis & factis Christi & Apostolorum extra Scripturam sacram nihil ad nos pervenisse potest, nisi ex testimonio eorum hominum, qui primis post Christum saeculis in Ecclesia floruerunt, & Apostolis ac viris Apostolicis successerunt: quales sunt illi quos Patres antiquos hodie nominamus, & quorum monumenta inter Christianos supersunt. At omnes illi fuerunt errori obnoxii, & tales ipsi se fatentur, cupiuntque ut scripta sua ad Scripturae normam exigantur; non vero recipiantur ἀθεωρήτως & sine examine. Imo ipsi Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae non paucos errores & naevos in iis annotarunt: idque non tantum quum aliquis eorum solitarius, ut sic dicam, loquitur, aliis tacentibus, vel contra dicentibus: Sed etiam quum eorum plurimi in idem consentiunt, quod multis exemplis potest fieri manifestum. Sic, ex. gr. plerique patres docuerunt animas sanctorum ante resurrectionem divinae visionis gloria frui non posse, ut notat Sixtus Senensis, Bibliothecae sanctae lib. 6. annotatione 365. ubi prolixe citat in hanc rem testimonia Justini, Tertulliani, Clementis, Origenis, Lactantii, Victorini, Ambrosii, Prudentii, Augustini, Theodoreti, & multorum recentiorum. Ejusdem quoque libri annot. 35. observat Veteres sensisse nullam creaturam esse incorpoream, & dogma istud illis sic placuisse, ut inter Catholicas regulas & synodicas sanctiones receptum fuerit. Annotatione vero 26. adducit multa loca Chrysostomi, Origenis, Athanasii, Hilarii, Ambrosii, Hieronymi, Chromatii Episcopi Aquileiensis, Oecumenii, Euthymii, unde probat illos credidisse omne juramentum esse simpliciter illicitum, & Christianis interdictum. Praeterea error fuit apud antiquissimos Patres valde solennis, Christum in terris olim aliquandiu cum sanctis in carne regnaturum: quod sensisse olim Papiam Episcopum Hierapolitanum, Irenaeum, Apollinarium, Tertullianum, Lactantium, Severum & Victorinum, testis est Hieronymus, lib. de viris illustribus in Papia, & libro undecimo in Prophetam Ezechielem. Neque Hieron. ipse & Augustinus audent sententiam istam aperte damnare, ut agnoscit idem Sixtus lib. 5. annot. 19. Denique in eodem lib. annot. 171. refert testimonia Origenis, Ambrosii, Hilarii, Basilii, Lactantii, Hieronymi, unde liquet illos existimavisse omnes homines qui sunt qui fuerunt & qui futuri sunt, uno Christo excepto, examinandos, probandos, & aliquo modo urendos igne conflagrationis mundanae in die judicii. Cum ergo prisci illi Ecclesiae Doctores ita fuerint errori obnoxii, ut dogma falsum atque erroneum ceu veritatem divinam amplecti potuerint, quomodo Ecclesiae posteriorum saeculorum tam certe esse possunt traditiones illae quas nonnisi ex eorum fide & testimonio didicit, atque illud quod consignatum videt in divinis ipsis libris Prophetarum & Apostolorum? Et annon omnino a recta ratione abhorret illud, quod testantur homines qui fallere & falli potuerunt, debere apud Ecclesiam authoritatem parem obtinere cum eo quod Deus ipse per Apostolos & Prophetas testatur?
pass_a_gloss: And certainly how undeservedly unwritten traditions are equated in authority with Scripture is plain from this: that in the sacred Scriptures divinely inspired writers, placed beyond all danger of error, testify to us that the Lord Christ taught and instituted this and that. But concerning the sayings and deeds of Christ and the Apostles outside sacred Scripture nothing can have reached us except from the testimony of those men who flourished in the Church in the first centuries after Christ and succeeded the Apostles and apostolic men: such are those whom we today name the ancient Fathers, and whose monuments survive among Christians. But all of them were liable to error, and they themselves confess themselves such, and desire that their writings be measured by the norm of Scripture; and not that they be received ἀθεωρήτως and without examination. Indeed the doctors of the Roman Church themselves have noted not a few errors and blemishes in them: and that not only when one of them speaks alone, so to speak, while others are silent or contradict; but also when many of them agree in the same thing, which can be made plain by many examples. Thus, for example, most of the fathers taught that the souls of the saints cannot enjoy the glory of the divine vision before the resurrection, as Sixtus of Siena notes in Bibliotheca sancta book 6, annotation 365, where he cites at length on this matter the testimonies of Justin, Tertullian, Clement, Origen, Lactantius, Victorinus, Ambrose, Prudentius, Augustine, Theodoret, and many more recent writers. Also in annotation 35 of the same book he observes that the ancients thought no creature is incorporeal, and that that dogma so pleased them that it was received among Catholic rules and synodical sanctions. And in annotation 26 he brings many places of Chrysostom, Origen, Athanasius, Hilary, Ambrose, Jerome, Chromatius bishop of Aquileia, Oecumenius, and Euthymius, from which he proves they believed every oath simply illicit and forbidden to Christians. Besides, a very solemn error among the most ancient Fathers was that Christ would someday reign for a while on earth with the saints in the flesh: which Papias bishop of Hierapolis, Irenaeus, Apollinaris, Tertullian, Lactantius, Severus, and Victorinus once held, as Jerome witnesses in On Illustrious Men on Papias, and in book 11 on the prophet Ezekiel. Neither Jerome himself nor Augustine dare openly condemn that opinion, as the same Sixtus acknowledges in book 5, annotation 19. Finally in the same book, annotation 171, he reports testimonies of Origen, Ambrose, Hilary, Basil, Lactantius, and Jerome, from which it is clear they thought all people who are, were, and will be — Christ alone excepted — are to be examined, proved, and in some way burned by the fire of the world's conflagration on the day of judgment. Since therefore those early doctors of the Church were so liable to error that they could embrace a false and erroneous dogma as divine truth, how can the traditions of the Church of later ages be so certain — traditions she has learned only from their faith and testimony — and be set beside what she sees consigned in the divine books of the Prophets and Apostles themselves? And does it not wholly revolt from right reason that what men who could deceive and be deceived testify should obtain equal authority in the Church with what God Himself testifies through Apostles and Prophets?
pass_b_english: Unwritten traditions are wrongly leveled with Scripture: Scripture's inspired writers, beyond error's reach, tell us what Christ taught and instituted.
Outside Scripture, sayings and deeds of Christ and the Apostles reach us only through early post-apostolic witnesses — the Fathers whose monuments remain.
Those Fathers were fallible, confessed it, and asked that their writings be measured by Scripture — not received ἀθεωρήτως and without examination.
Roman doctors themselves mark many errors and blemishes in the Fathers — not only in lone opinions, but even where many agree.

Examples Sixtus of Siena collects: most Fathers denied the saints the beatific vision before the resurrection; ancients held no creature incorporeal as a received Catholic rule; many forbade all oaths; chiliast hope of an earthly fleshly reign (Papias, Irenaeus, and others); and a purifying world-fire for all except Christ on judgment day — which even Jerome and Augustine hesitate to condemn outright.

If early doctors could hug false dogma as divine truth, later-age traditions learned only from their witness cannot stand as certain beside what God consigned in the Prophets' and Apostles' books — nor can fallible men's testimony claim equal Church authority with God's own.
